awake.verb type: action — dynamic, and literary beside everyday *wake up*; keep the verb apart from the adjective *awake* (*I was awake at four* is a state, not a past tense)
awake.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when you stop sleeping (*she awoke to the sound of rain*), transitive when you rouse someone or stir a feeling (*the sirens awoke half the neighborhood*); *awake to* takes a prepositional object
awake.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *half the neighborhood was awoken by the sirens*, *an old homesickness has been awoken*. No passive of the intransitive *she awoke*.

bear.verb type: action — dynamic in the carrying, enduring, and producing senses; closer to **stative** in *bear a name / bear a resemblance / bear interest*, where the progressive is odd: ✗ *the building is bearing her name*
bear.transitivity: **both** — transitive almost everywhere (*bear the cost*, *bear three children*, *bear fruit*), intransitive in the direction sense (*bear left where the road forks*)
bear.passive: **restricted** — natural for costs and burdens (*the legal fees have been borne by the company*), and *be born* is passive-only (*she was born in Ohio*; there is no active ✗ *she borned*). But the name and resemblance senses resist it: ✗ *her grandfather's name is borne by the building*, and ✗ *left was borne at the fork*.

bespeak.verb type: **stative** in its one living American sense, "be evidence of" — the subject is a thing, not an actor, and the progressive is out: ✗ *the silence is bespeaking trouble*. The archaic "order in advance" sense is action
bespeak.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory: *cracked paint bespeaks neglect*, ✗ *the empty shelves bespoke*
bespeak.passive: **restricted** — fine in the archaic ordering sense (*the rooms had been bespoken months before the wedding*), but the evidence sense resists it like other stative verbs: ✗ *neglect is bespoken by the cracked paint*.

bite.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, from teeth (*the terrier bit the mail carrier*) to tires gripping snow to cold and tariffs taking hold
bite.transitivity: **both** — transitive with an object (*bite your tongue*, *bite back a laugh*), intransitive with the object left out (*dogs bite*, *nobody bit*, *the wind bites*)
bite.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *she was bitten by a spider in the garage*. No passive of the intransitive *trout bite best after sunrise*.

break.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative: the same event runs transitive or intransitive (*he broke the vase* / *the vase broke*). Bare *broke* also lives on as an adjective, "out of money"
break.transitivity: **both** — transitive when someone breaks a thing, a rule, or a record (*she broke the state record*), intransitive of things that break, fail, or begin (*my phone broke*, *day breaks around five*, *war broke out*)
break.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the window had been broken before we arrived*, *the story was broken on Sunday*. No passive of the intransitive *day breaks* or *the talks broke down*.

choose.verb type: action — dynamic mental verb; the progressive is fine (*I'm still choosing*). The participle *chosen* also stands alone as an elevated adjective: *the chosen one*
choose.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the thing picked (*they chose the cheaper apartment*), intransitive when the object is understood (*you choose this time*) or replaced by *between / from* or a *to*-infinitive (*she chose to walk*)
choose.passive: **yes** — *she was chosen from a field of forty*, *a captain is chosen every September*. The *to*-infinitive pattern has no passive: ✗ *to walk was chosen by her*.

cleave.verb type: action — dynamic in both of the unrelated verbs that share this spelling, splitting and clinging; note that modern American English inflects both regularly (*cleaved*), with *clove/cloven* frozen in *cloven hoof*
cleave.transitivity: **both** — transitive when you split something (*one blow clove the log in two*, *the jet cleaves the air*), intransitive with a preposition in *cleave to* (*he cleaved to the old customs*)
cleave.passive: **restricted** — the splitting sense passivizes (*the old oak had been cloven from crown to root*), but *cleave to* is prepositional and resists it: ✗ *the plan is cleaved to by her*.

delve.verb type: action — dynamic; a digging verb that today survives almost entirely in the figurative *delve into*, with the strong forms *dolve/dolven* archaic
delve.transitivity: **intransitive** in all living American uses — the complement is a prepositional phrase, not an object: *she delved into the archive*, *he delved in his coat for the tickets*. Only the archaic literal sense took a direct object (*the gardener dolve a trench*)
delve.passive: **no** in modern usage — an intransitive verb has nothing to promote, and the prepositional passive is marginal at best: ✗ *his tax records have been delved into*. Only the archaic transitive digging sense allows one: *the well had been dolven long before the abbey*.

forbear.verb type: action — dynamic, though what it describes is deliberate inaction; formal and prefixed, where Americans say *hold back* or *refrain*
forbear.transitivity: **intransitive** in practice — it takes *from* + -ing, a bare infinitive, or nothing at all (*he forbore to answer*, *the neighbors forbore for years*); the rare direct object (*she has forborne every provocation*) is literary
forbear.passive: **no** — with a *from*-phrase or an infinitive there is nothing to promote, and even the rare direct object refuses it: ✗ *every provocation was forborne*, ✗ *the loan was forborne on*.

forget.verb type: action — dynamic in the sense of an event that happens to you rather than one you perform; the progressive is limited but possible (*I'm forgetting names lately*). *Forget it* is a frozen imperative
forget.transitivity: **transitive** — the object may be a noun (*forget your badge*), a clause (*I forget where I parked*), or a *to*-infinitive (*don't forget to lock the door*); it is left out only in fixed uses
forget.passive: **restricted** — natural with a noun object (*the whole affair had been forgotten by then*, *his name has been forgotten*), impossible with an infinitive or clause complement: ✗ *to set the alarm was forgotten by him*.

forswear.verb type: action — dynamic and performative: saying it is doing it. Formal and legal; *forsworn* also works as an adjective, and a *forsworn witness* is a perjurer, not a renouncer
forswear.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory — a noun, an -ing form, or a reflexive pronoun: *they forswore cash payments*, *a man who forswears himself in court*; ✗ *he forswore* on its own
forswear.passive: **restricted** — possible in the renouncing sense but rare and formal (*private property is forsworn here*), and the reflexive perjury sense has none: ✗ *himself was forsworn by the witness*.

freeze.verb type: action — dynamic and ergative (*the pond froze* / *she froze the berries*); *frozen* does heavy duty as an adjective (*frozen peas*, *a frozen account*)
freeze.transitivity: **both** — intransitive of ice, people, and software (*the pond froze solid*, *my laptop has frozen*), transitive of food, money, and rates (*the board voted to freeze tuition*)
freeze.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *regulators have frozen the firm's assets* → *the firm's assets have been frozen*, *small vendors have been frozen out of the market*. No passive of the intransitive *the ground had frozen*.

hide.verb type: action — dynamic, whether deliberate (*he hid the key*) or not (*clouds hide the summit*); *hidden* is also a common adjective, as in *hidden fees*
hide.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a thing or fact concealed (*the report hid the real numbers*), intransitive when you conceal yourself (*she hid in the stairwell*, *they hid out for a week*)
hide.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the path had been hidden by new snow*, *the remote has been hidden again*. No passive of the intransitive *the cat hid under the porch*.

interweave.verb type: action — dynamic; in real American prose the participle *interwoven* does most of the work, as an adjective (*interwoven storylines*) or a predicate (*the two economies are deeply interwoven*)
interweave.transitivity: **both** — normally transitive (*the artist interwove copper wire and silk thread*, *good novels interweave several lives*), occasionally intransitive of the strands themselves (*the two plots have interwoven so tightly you cannot follow one alone*)
interweave.passive: **yes** — *the two fibers have been interwoven for centuries*, *three folk melodies are interwoven in the score*; the passive and the adjectival participle are where this verb actually lives.

misspeak.verb type: action — dynamic, and in American public life nearly frozen in the first-person past: *I misspoke* concedes an error while denying intent
misspeak.transitivity: **both** — usually intransitive (*if I misspeak, please correct me*), transitive in the older plain sense of getting a word out wrong (*the announcer misspoke the winner's name*)
misspeak.passive: **restricted** — marginal even with an object (?*the winner's name was misspoken on live television*), and the ordinary intransitive use has no passive at all: ✗ *it was misspoken by the senator*.

speak.verb type: action — dynamic in the talking senses (*he spoke for twenty minutes*), but **stative** when it means knowing a language, where the progressive is out: ✗ *I am speaking Spanish* to mean you know it
speak.transitivity: **both** — intransitive at the core (*please speak more slowly*, *nobody had spoken for a minute*), transitive with a language or a fixed object (*we speak Spanish at home*, *she speaks her mind*)
speak.passive: **restricted** — natural with a language or a fixed object (*Spanish is spoken here*, *not a word was spoken*), but the ordinary intransitive and prepositional uses have none: ✗ *the landlord was spoken*, and ✗ *she was spoken to slowly* only works as the separate prepositional passive.

steal.verb type: action — dynamic; the taking senses and the quiet-movement sense (*she stole out of the house*) share one form but behave differently
steal.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the thing taken (*someone stole my umbrella*; you steal the thing but rob the person: ✗ *they stole the bank*), intransitive with *from* or a direction (*big labels steal from small ones*, *fog steals up the valley*)
steal.passive: **yes** in the taking senses, and this is where the participle error shows: *two paintings have been stolen from the museum*, ✗ *my bike has been stole*. No passive of the movement sense: ✗ *out of the house was stolen*.

swear.verb type: action — dynamic in both unrelated senses, taking an oath and using profanity; *sworn* also serves as an adjective (*a sworn statement*, *sworn testimony*)
swear.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the profanity sense and with *at / by / off* (*he swore at the referee*, *my mother swears by this cough syrup*), transitive with an oath, a clause, or a person (*they swore an oath*, *I swear I locked the door*, *they swear in the new council Monday*)
swear.passive: **yes** in the oath senses, and usually preferred there — *the jury had been sworn in before lunch*, *witnesses are sworn before testifying*. The profanity sense allows only the prepositional passive (*the referee was sworn at*), and *swear by* refuses it: ✗ *that mechanic was sworn by*.

tear.verb type: action — dynamic and ergative (*he tore the letter* / *the seam tore*); the fast-movement sense (*he tore out of the driveway*) is a separate informal use, and *tear* /tɛr/ is a different word from the noun *tear* /tɪr/
tear.transitivity: **both** — transitive when you rip or wrench something (*she tore the page out of the notebook*, *he tore a ligament*), intransitive when the fabric gives way or someone moves fast (*my jacket has torn at the elbow*, *kids tear around the yard*)
tear.passive: **yes** in the ripping senses — *the awning had been torn loose by the storm*. *Be torn between* is passive-only, with no active counterpart: *I am torn between the two offers*, ✗ *the two offers tear me between*. No passive of the movement sense.

unfreeze.verb type: action — dynamic and ergative like its base *freeze* (*the court unfroze the accounts* / *the line has unfrozen*); in practice the base and the participle carry the verb, and the finite past *unfroze* reads oddly to many Americans
unfreeze.transitivity: **both** — transitive of funds, rates, and screens (*sanctions relief would unfreeze billions*, *a restart usually unfreezes the screen*), intransitive of the thing thawing on its own (*the line has unfrozen*)
unfreeze.passive: **yes** — *the hiring budget had been unfrozen weeks before anyone noticed*, *the family's accounts were unfrozen in April*; the participle also stands as an adjective (*the funds are still unfrozen*).

wake.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative between sleeping and rousing (*she woke twice* / *the thunder woke the baby*). Nothing to do with the slang adjective *woke*
wake.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when you stop sleeping (*I wake at six without an alarm*), transitive when you rouse a person or a feeling (*the song woke something in her*); *wake up* works both ways
wake.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the baby was woken by the thunder*, *we had been woken before the alarm went off*. No passive of the intransitive *she woke twice in the night*.

wear.verb type: **both** — the erosion senses are action and dynamic (*water wore a channel through the rock*), while having clothes on is closer to **stative**, a state that happens to allow the progressive for temporary wear (*she's wearing boots today*). *Worn* is also an adjective meaning shabby or tired
wear.transitivity: **both** — transitive with clothing, a look, or a surface (*he wore the same tie*, *traffic wears the paint off*), intransitive when the thing itself deteriorates or an effect fades (*cheap fabric wears badly*, *the numbness wears off*)
wear.passive: **restricted** — free in the erosion senses (*the stairs had been worn smooth*, *he was worn down by the campaign*), but the clothing sense is stilted as a full passive (✗ *the same tie was worn by him to every interview*) and survives mainly as a reduced participle: *the coat worn by the bride*.

weave.verb type: action — dynamic, and the sense picks the forms: making cloth or storylines takes *wove/woven*, while winding through traffic is regular — ✓ *the cab weaved across three lanes*, ✗ *the cab wove across three lanes*
weave.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the making senses (*her grandmother wove blankets*, *he weaves jokes into serious lectures*), intransitive in the movement sense (*cyclists weave through stopped traffic*)
weave.passive: **yes** in the making senses — *the scarf is woven from two kinds of wool*, *the letters had been woven into the narrative*. No passive of the movement sense: ✗ *through the pack was weaved*.
